title: Impact of AI Tools on Learning Outcomes: Decreasing Knowledge and Over-Reliance
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether allowing students to use generative AI tools in a university course improves performance at the cost of genuine learning. The authors situate the study in a broader debate where some prior work reports positive effects of AI on learning, while other work suggests AI may promote cognitive offloading, disengagement, and reduced critical thinking. Their central question is whether unrestricted AI use in authentic, grade-bearing educational settings leads students to substitute AI output for knowledge acquisition.

The study reports a randomized experiment conducted in an operations research course in a Business Informatics program at Corvinus University of Budapest. Students were randomly assigned within seminar groups, stratified by gender, either to an AI-permitted condition or an offline condition that prohibited AI use during tests by using an offline computer lab. Both groups could use static offline materials. The design included two midterms, a final computer-based exam, and a key offline paper-based true/false test intended to measure actual understanding. A point-compensation scheme was introduced so that the lower-performing group would receive score adjustments to equalize average performance, in an effort to address fairness concerns.

The population was undergraduate students in a single university course in Hungary, with approximately 100-120 students enrolled. The setting was primarily a classroom/computer-lab course with weekly seminars and periodic lectures. However, the experiment was disrupted by strong student complaints, media attention, and intervention from university and government actors. As a result, before the final exam the treatment and control groups were merged, all students were allowed to use AI on the final exam, and students could also discard earlier midterm scores if beneficial. This substantially weakened the original treatment contrast.

Despite this disruption, the authors conclude that uncontrolled AI use is associated with low engagement, over-reliance, and weak underlying knowledge. The AI group outperformed the offline group on the two midterms, but students' offline true/false scores were very low overall, suggesting poor mastery of course content. The authors interpret the paper test, ranking analyses, regression results, and sampled AI-detection checks as evidence that many students relied heavily on AI rather than learning the material. They argue that unrestricted AI in demanding subjects can reduce knowledge acquisition, while also highlighting the ethical, legal, and perceptual difficulties of running randomized educational experiments involving AI access.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools/LLM assistants used by students to solve course tasks and exams; the paper mentions examples such as ChatGPT but studies unrestricted generative AI use as a category rather than a single product.
identified_tools.use_case: University students in an operations research course were randomly assigned to an AI-permitted group versus an offline no-AI group for classes and exams; the study examined performance, offline true/false knowledge test results, score alignment, and over-reliance on AI.

findings.finding_summary: In the randomized course experiment, the AI-permitted group scored higher than the offline group on the first midterm (12.64 vs. 10.93; difference 1.71; p=0.015) and second midterm (11.51 vs. 5.93; difference 5.58; p<0.001). On the final exam, after the groups were merged and all students were allowed AI, the difference was not statistically significant (40.48 vs. 41.53; difference -1.05; p=0.734).
findings.measure: Operations research course assessment scores: first midterm, second midterm, and final exam
findings.sample_size: varied by assessment: first midterm n=93 (45 AI, 48 offline); second midterm n=92 (44 AI, 48 offline); final exam n=95 (46 AI, 49 offline)

findings.finding_summary: The paper’s main interpretation is that uncontrolled generative AI use reduced genuine knowledge acquisition. On the offline paper true/false test administered at the final exam, students’ knowledge was estimated to be no more than 20 correct answers out of 50 (40%), with realistic knowledge levels closer to 20% or lower; the authors state this implies a likely knowledge drop of at least 20 percentage points compared with previous years.
findings.measure: Offline 50-item true/false paper test of basic understanding; modeled knowledge level from test performance
findings.effect_size: likely decrease of 20–40 percentage points (authors’ estimate)
findings.sample_size: n=95 (46 AI, 49 offline) for paper test

findings.finding_summary: Hypothesis 1 was not supported: on the offline paper true/false test, the AI group slightly outperformed the offline group (30.08 vs. 27.71 correct-answer metric; difference 2.37; p=0.011), but the authors argue this result was confounded by the last-minute merger of groups before the final exam. They interpret the higher AI-group paper score as random fluctuation rather than evidence of better learning.
findings.measure: Paper true/false test scores during final exam

findings.finding_summary: Support for Hypothesis 2 indicated weaker alignment between demonstrated knowledge and assessed performance for AI-permitted students. Linear regression showed very low explanatory power of midterm/final scores for paper-test knowledge in the AI group (R2=0.145; first midterm coefficient 0.573, p<0.05; second midterm coefficient -0.157; final exam coefficient -0.031), while the offline group showed somewhat stronger alignment (R2=0.253; second midterm coefficient 0.639, p<0.01; final exam coefficient 0.132).
findings.measure: Alignment between paper true/false knowledge test and other course scores; SRD and linear regression
findings.sample_size: n=43 AI; n=47 offline in regression

findings.finding_summary: The authors conclude that uncontrolled AI use led to disengagement, low understanding, and over-reliance. They report that a 20% sample of final exams assessed with CopyLeaks showed exorbitant AI reliance, with a median detected AI content of 100% in both groups.
findings.measure: AI reliance/AI-generated content in sampled final exam responses
findings.effect_size: median 100% AI content in both groups
findings.sample_size: n=20 sampled tests (10 from each group)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment in an authentic university course, which strengthens causal inference, but the intervention was substantially compromised when the groups were merged before the final exam. The paper still reports primary comparative data, yet the protocol disruption creates important validity concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s central claim is negative: uncontrolled generative AI use decreased knowledge and promoted over-reliance. Although some assessment-score differences favored the AI group, the authors interpret the main educational impact as harmful rather than beneficial.
